subject: English
summaryPoints: Modal verbs (must, have to, should, ought to, can, could, may, might, shall, will) express functions such as obligation, prohibition, necessity, permission, advice, and logical deduction.
'Must' denotes strong personal obligation originating from the speaker or logical necessity, whereas 'have to' denotes external obligation imposed by external regulations or laws.
'Must not' ('mustn't') conveys strict prohibition (actions not allowed), whereas 'don't have to' or 'need not' conveys absence of obligation (action is optional, not mandatory).
'Should' and 'ought to' express moral duty, recommendation, or advice; 'ought to' is followed by a to-infinitive.
Dummy auxiliary 'do/does' and their negative forms 'don't/doesn't' function in negation and interrogative structures in simple present tense.
Informal letter format consists of six core components: sender's address, date, salutation, body (introduction, main content, conclusion), subscription/complimentary close, and writer's name.

formulas.label: Modal Auxiliary Construction
formulas.expr: Subject + Modal Verb + Bare Infinitive (V1 base) + Object/Complement

formulas.label: Prohibition Formula
formulas.expr: Subject + must not (mustn't) + Bare Infinitive (V1)  [Meaning: It is forbidden/illegal]

formulas.label: Absence of Obligation Formula
formulas.expr: Subject + do/does not have to + Bare Infinitive (V1)  OR  Subject + need not (needn't) + Bare Infinitive (V1)

formulas.label: Advice / Recommendation Structure
formulas.expr: Subject + should + Bare Infinitive (V1)  OR  Subject + ought to + Bare Infinitive (V1)

examTip: A major EUEE trap is confusing 'mustn't' with 'don't have to'. Remember: 'You mustn't drive through a red light' means it is illegal and forbidden, while 'You don't have to carry an umbrella' means it is not necessary, but you may if you want.

keyDefinitions.definition: A helping verb that alters the mood or modality of the main verb to denote ability, permission, obligation, possibility, or deduction.
A grammatical decree or rule enforcing that an action is strictly forbidden and must not be performed.
A word or phrase that has the identical or nearly equivalent meaning as another word in the same language.
A word that denotes the exact opposite or contrary meaning of another specified word.

eueeFocusTopics: Distinction between prohibition ('mustn't') and lack of obligation ('don't have to')
Modal verbs of advice ('should' vs 'ought to')
Logical deduction modals ('must be' vs 'can't be')
Correct formatting and register of informal letters
Vocabulary of road safety, synonyms, and antonyms
